questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: My main motivation to on exchange was an ambition to improve my language skills, specifically my Italian.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose my destination (Bologna, IT) firstly because it would give me the opportunity to gain proficiency in Italian and secondly because it was rumoured to be characterised by a vivid and buzzing student culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy to find the necessary information upon arrival. I followed the instructions in Mobility Online and those which I received via email from my host university. When I was in doubt or needed further assistance, my Erasmus-supervisor and the International Mobility Office were quick to respond to my emails.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I conferred both with my Erasmus-supervisor and the International Mobility Office about my Confirmation of Arrival and my Learning Agreement. I further requested advice and support regarding my courses in Italian from my Erasmus-supervisor who very kindly arranged a meeting with me.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
In the beginning, I was very confused about the options available to me but through a meeting with the International Mobility Office, I discovered SAIS, an agency approved by the university which seeks to aid incoming students in their search for accomodation. On their website,
https://www.saisaccommodation.it/
, I created a profile seeking housing within the city walls and contacted several landlords. I was, however, very quickly contacted myself by a kind landlady whose apartment met all my criteria (though it was a bit more expensive than expected). I feared it was a scam, but upon my request I was put into contact with the tenants living in the apartment at the time who confirmed to me that the apartment was both real and good. I would definitely recommend SAIS to any future exchange students as I was very satisfied with the housing I found through their website.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Expect relatively high prices if you want to live inside the city walls and within walking distance of the university (I paid more in rent in Bologna than I do in Copenhagen, around 850 euros excluding utilities for a shared three-bedroom apartment with all facilities except aircon in-house). Expect also to find landlords who only speak Italian. Further, stay alert and find a place with airconditioning if possible as temperatures during the summer can easily surpass 38 degrees and the city is cursed with exceptionally high humidity.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I am personally very satisfied with the proces of finding housing and my actual accomodation, but I know others who have struggled to do the same.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The required check-in at the University of Bologna is easy enough in itself, requiring only a show of identity documents and flight/train tickets, but it took some asking around to discover that it can only be done online via a Teams meeting and only during certain time slots. These time slots were very limited compared to the number of incoming students so I required two attempts to get through to the Office because of the digital queue.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Upon arrival, I was required to check in via the Virtual Desk of the Incoming Exchange Student Desk. I received instructions to do so, the appropriate link to the Virtual Desk and information about the opening hours via the email I was assigned by the host university. After the check-in, which required a passport/other identity document and my flight ticket, I received a confirmation email, a certificate of attendance showing the start date of my mobility (though not the final end date) and instructions to fill out an online study plan, including all pre-approved courses I intended to take.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Links to online information pages were provided in the emails and I believe it was possible to contact the Incoming Exchange Student Desk, though I did not need to.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed to get a spot in all the classes I wanted as soon as I had discovered which classes had compatible schedules. I simply enrolled in them myself on a platform called Virtuale. The proces was explained to me by several very helpful professors during the first class.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Expect to check in online and expect waiting time at the Virtual Desk.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In my opinion, all courses roughly corresponded to the level of difficulty at my home university in their contents. I did, however, find the courses taught in Italian very lingustically challenging, especially in the beginning, as I was only at a B1-level in Italian when I arrived.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching is more conservative than at the University of Copenhagen. Expect listening more than discussion and oral mnemonic exams rather than written essays.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Introduction to Italian Culture, Anglo-American Literature 2, Storia delle Donne e di Genere nel Medioevo & Storia Medievale.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I found it very challenging to sit through lectures in Italian Culture as the classes were large, the hall stuffy and lacking in oxygen, the scheduled time late and my fellow students exceptionally prone to chatter, laughter and inconcentration. If you enjoy discussion and opportunities for participation, I would, instead, recommend "Storia delle Donne e di Genere nel Medioevo", taught by Prof. Giacomo Vignodelli. It required an oral presentation, contained opportunities for class discussion and was completed upon the construction of a short essay which must be summarised at the final oral exam. Overall, however, all professors were very welcoming and accomodating.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not expect housing to require such big spending (1700 euro rent, 1500 euro deposit, plus utilities) but felt it was worth it. I also did not expect to pay so much to travel (I visited other Italian towns at least twice, if not thrice a month). Also, beers, events and restaurants quickly devour huge sums of money due to the temptingly low prices (75-100 dkk for a lasagna at a nice restaurant)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Rent was higher than I expected of Italy but groceries and restaraunts were lower.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I have discovered no bars, trips or other non-academic events arranged by the University for the students, whether they be exchange or resident students, if you are not part of a club/society connected to the campus. There are, however, mailing lists offering participation in certain cultural events (bordering on academic activities) and oppportunities to receive discounts on f.x. cinema or train tickets. Due to my lack of interest, I do not know of any athletic initiatives.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would highly recommend a membership in the local ESN (Erasmus Student Network) which organises events, trips and other activities which enable you to meet other exchange students. The membership costs 5 euros and gives you the opportunity to sign up for a whole host of events, free or requiring the payment of a fee. The payments via bank transfer are difficult so show up at their office in Via Delle Belle Arti which is open for a few hours twice a week - and come early (!) as there is usually a long queue. Otherwise, I can recommend sports as I know of several people who have made friends by playing tennis or football in local clubs. This is especially important if you want to make local friends - that required proactiveness!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I have enjoyed many day trips, f.x. to Ravenna (mosaics), Ferrara (world's oldest wine bar), Venice (obvious reasons), Parma (raw horsemeat), Garda (cheap public ferry rides), Milan (the Sforza castle and the Olympics), Naples (Pompei and the Royal Palace) and Modena (the Bucket which you must look up) - all of which are reachable by train. When it gets hot, go to the beach at Riccione, Ravenna or Rimini, to the Garda Lake or to Marzabotto which is close to a lovely spot where you can bathe in the Reno. Otherwise, enjoy the good food at f.x. Dell'Orsa or Trattoria Da Me and the warm summernights and the nightlife, f.x. at Piedra del Sol or Cassero (which has free entry on Wednesdays).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy as I had lived in Rome before.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: You must be extremely proactive. Seek out sports clubs, cultural events or invite fellow students out directly. My general impression is that you otherwise often end up only moving in Erasmus circles.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It is important to remember the more formal nature of Italian university relationships, making sure to use appropriate language rather than calling professors by their first names. Exams are also structured differently than in Denmark, with no fixed schedules and other students or professors sometimes present in the same room. Stay updated via the Unibo app and the online platform for students, Studenti Online. You must also enroll yourself in the exams via AlmaEsami.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The general openness, relaxation and loose sense of timeliness.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Save money for housing within the city walls: it will be more expensive but worth it, especially in the heat. Find a place with aircon or buy a fan: you will need it by May or June. Be proactive about making new friendships, especially if you want them to be with locals: Join clubs, play sports or chat someone up on in class or at a bar.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Always check both the email inbox of your host and your home university and don't be afraid to seek help from professors and administration offices - they are all very friendly.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Improving my Italian to a point where I passed two exams in Italian with top marks.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding local friends and other exchange students with advanced Italian to share my learning journey with.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
